title: How the urinary system works
intro: The urinary system filters waste and excess water from your blood and removes them as urine. It includes the kidneys, the ureters, the bladder and the urethra. Knowing how these parts work together makes it easier to understand common problems such as infections, stones or bladder control difficulties, and to talk about them with a healthcare professional.

sections.heading: The kidneys: filtering the blood
paragraphs: You have two kidneys, each about the size of a fist, located on either side of the spine below the ribs. Together they filter all of your blood many times a day. Tiny filtering units remove waste products, extra salts and surplus water while keeping what the body needs, such as proteins and most nutrients.

Besides making urine, the kidneys help regulate blood pressure, balance minerals such as sodium and potassium, keep the blood at the right level of acidity, and produce hormones that support red blood cell production and bone health. Because they do so many jobs, kidney problems can affect the whole body.

sections.heading: From the kidneys to the bladder
paragraphs: Urine collects in a funnel-shaped area inside each kidney and then flows down a thin muscular tube called the ureter. Gentle, wave-like muscle contractions push the urine along, so it keeps moving even when you are lying down. Each ureter enters the bladder at an angle that helps stop urine from flowing backward.

If something blocks a ureter, such as a kidney stone, urine can back up and cause pain, often described as sudden and cramp-like in the side or back. Doctors take such symptoms seriously because a blockage combined with infection can harm the kidney.

sections.heading: Storing and releasing urine
paragraphs: The bladder is a stretchy, muscular organ that stores urine until it is convenient to empty it. As it fills, nerves send signals to the brain, and most adults first feel the urge to pass urine when the bladder holds a few hundred millilitres. A healthy bladder can hold urine for several hours without leaking.

When you decide to urinate, the brain signals the bladder muscle to contract and the sphincter muscles around the outlet to relax. The urine then leaves the body through the urethra. The urethra is shorter in women than in men, which is one reason bladder infections are more common in women.

sections.heading: Common problems
paragraphs: Typical problems include urinary tract infections, kidney and bladder stones, an overactive bladder, leaking urine when coughing or exercising, and in men, difficulty emptying the bladder because of an enlarged prostate. Symptoms may include burning when passing urine, needing to go often or urgently, blood in the urine, or pain in the side or lower abdomen.

Many of these conditions are treatable. Blood in the urine, fever with back pain, or being unable to pass urine at all should be checked promptly, because they can signal something that needs urgent attention.

sections.heading: Looking after your urinary health
paragraphs: Drinking enough fluids, usually a little more when it is hot or when you are active, helps keep urine diluted and flushes the system. Not holding urine for very long periods, emptying the bladder fully and practising good hygiene may lower the risk of infection.

Managing blood pressure and blood sugar protects the kidneys over the long term, and care is needed with some painkillers and other medicines that can strain them. Regular check-ups matter more if you have diabetes, high blood pressure or a family history of kidney disease.

examples.title: Noticing changes early
examples.text: Imagine you have started needing the toilet much more often at night, and passing urine sometimes burns. You could keep a short note of how often you go and how much you drink for a few days, then bring it to your appointment so the clinician can see the pattern and decide whether a urine test is useful.

examples.title: Talking about leaking
examples.text: Suppose you leak a little urine when you laugh or lift something, and you feel embarrassed. You might practise describing exactly when it happens and how it affects your day, then ask whether pelvic floor training or other options could help, knowing that this is a common and treatable problem.
